academy.script: Merit Point Academy connects classroom learning with research for secondary-school students. Our mission is wholehearted service to students. That means starting with each student's interests and readiness, supporting authentic work they can explain, and building lasting ability through practice and feedback. AI tools and interdisciplinary projects support this process. We want students to become more independent as they learn. What is one question you would enjoy investigating?

history.script: Our programs grew from students' needs. Around twenty twenty-five, Xiwang Guo at NJIT began free Sunday research mentoring for high-school students at Livingston Library. This gradually developed into structured one-to-one guidance, from choosing a question and finding data to analysis and writing. In summer twenty twenty-six, Bo Shang led two small AI Toolbox cohorts, with around fifteen lessons and no more than five students per group. After limited one-to-one Python teaching that summer, fall brought the formal launch of Python group classes. As the programs grew, support extended to the foundations students needed. A beginner can now start with Python, progress to AI Toolbox, and later pursue research with a mentor. The mission continues: help each student take the next step.

pathway.script: Merit Point Academy’s research growth pathway has three stages. Stage one is Python for AI Research. Students build programming, data analysis, and scientific computing foundations. Today, we are trying a small part of that first stage. Stage two is AI Toolbox: learn machine learning and other AI methods, follow a research process, read papers, and develop an AI project. Stage three is AI Research Mentorship: work with doctoral mentors on an individual research question, from literature and model design to experiments, analysis, and writing. A portfolio, poster, and presentation help communicate that work. The pathway welcomes beginners in grades eight through twelve. What question would you like to investigate as your skills grow?

phase-one.script: Our Python course has fifteen lessons, organized into four learning units. In lessons one through three, you learn to read and change a small program: variables and lists, decisions and loops, then reusable functions and research records. You also begin choosing a question of your own. Lessons four through eight build the evidence. Use NumPy for simulations, pandas for tables, and charts to explore a question. Keep reasons for your data-cleaning choices and plan how to test an idea. Each unit gives you something to build on. Today’s trial is a small taste of lesson one: predict, run, change, and explain.

syllabus-project.script: The second half of the Python course connects these foundations to a small research project. Lessons nine through thirteen introduce a machine-learning baseline, numerical and category predictions, decision trees, and fair model comparisons. Learn to inspect mistakes and compare methods on the same test. These are introductory modeling lessons within Python, preparing you for the broader AI Toolbox program. In lessons fourteen and fifteen, bring your question, code, figures, actual results, and limitations into a project others can check. Prepare an abstract and poster draft, present your work, and answer questions. You choose one small project and use the methods that fit its question.

question.script: Does scoring change with distance? Imagine taking practice shots from three, six, and nine meters away. Before seeing the results, make a prediction. Would the closest shots have the highest success rate, would the rates be similar, or do we need more information? Our data will be synthetic, which means invented for this lesson. A real investigation would need a fair comparison. Pause here, record your prediction, and name one condition you would try to keep similar, such as the player, the angle, or the number of attempts.

reveal.script: The original sample has three goals in five attempts, which is sixty percent. Replacing a miss with a goal gives four goals in five attempts, or eighty percent. Adding a new goal gives four goals in six attempts, or about sixty-six point seven percent. Both changes add one goal, but only the second adds an attempt. That is why the percentages differ. Compare these results with your prediction and explain the denominator in each case. If your prediction changed, record what you learned. Revising an explanation after checking evidence is useful research work.
